newsitem.title: USA: G7 leaders giving Yeltsin enhanced role at summit.
newsitem.headline: G7 leaders giving Yeltsin enhanced role at summit.

text.p: Leaders of the seven leading industrial countries welcome Russian President Boris Yeltsin to an enhanced role in their ranks this week in their annual economic summit.

Instead of the Group of Seven summit, all involved are calling it the "Summit of the Eight" in a symbolic gesture to stress Russia's integration. Yeltsin will be excluded from only one financial-related meeting in three days of summitry.

Denver, enjoying an economic revival thanks to high tech, was ecstatic that the world's attention was focused on the city. It has hung the national flags of all participants in the streets and assembled an army of 400,000 volunteers to greet visitors and ferry them around the city. Security was tight, with manhole covers nailed down.

In the mile-high atmosphere of this Rocky Mountain city, the leaders will focus on the world's major hotspots such as attempts to build a durable peace in Bosnia and reignite the Middle East peace process. They will also give a major push to promoting trade and investment in Africa to try to bring the sub-Sahara out of poverty.

President Bill Clinton, host of the summit, on Tuesday announced an economic development plan for Africa that cuts tariffs for countries that reform their economies and said he wanted the summit nations to join his effort. U.S. officials said they expected the eight to issue a statement pledging to coordinate efforts to help Africa avoid the type of conflicts that have led to the slaughter of tens of thousands of people.

The annual Group of Seven (G7) summit -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States -- will spend time on its founding purpose, to take stock of the world economy. The United States, Britain and Canada are enjoying strong growth while France, Germany and Italy suffer from sluggish domestic economies and double-digit unemployment.

France and Germany are divided over economic and monetary union (EMU) in Europe, with France's newly elected socialist government reluctant to commit itself to further austerity to meet the economic criteria for a single currency.
An issue expected to surface at bilateral meetings outside the summit will be plans to invite new members to join NATO.

The United States last week defied its allies, saying it wanted to invite only three nations -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin negotiations to join the Western alliance. France and Germany insist they will support Romania and Slovenia for membership as well despite the U.S. stance.

French President Jacques Chirac, who vaulted onto the world stage two years ago and dominated the Halifax, Nova Scotia, G7 summit, comes to this gathering greatly weakened after losing control of parliament to opposition Socialists in an election seen as a rebuke to his economic policies, which failed to put a dent in France's 12.8 percent unemployment.

Yeltsin, 66, missed last year's summit in Lyon, France, because of heart surgery after he was re-elected. He comes to Denver in better physical and political shape but still presiding over a country that has not come to terms with its new economic reality.

Clinton enjoys a booming U.S. economy and is pushing second-term initiatives on NATO expansion and balancing the U.S. budget. But he is dogged by embarrassing political scandals including a sexual harassment lawsit and a Senate probe into Democratic fund-raising tactics last year.
